scopeNotes: Unless a record says otherwise, a directed input is a strongly connected graph and an undirected input is a connected graph, with n vertices, m edges or arcs, and positive integer scalar weights in [1,n^{10}]. The catalog distinguishes word-operation improvements, classical high-accuracy bit complexity, and precision-sensitive entrywise, multiplicative-determinant or exact-integer guarantees. Inline mathematics is written in $...$ LaTeX. The word 'faster' is always relative to the named primary-source baseline; when a broad seed milestone is already achieved, the record states the sharpened remaining question.

polylogFactorImprovements.model: Complexities involving logarithmic factors are measured in word operations on O(log n)-bit words.

classicalPolynomialFactorImprovements.model: Polylogarithmic factors are suppressed. Bit complexity is acceptable, and the standard high-accuracy target is 1/poly(n) additive or normwise error.

entrywiseMultiplicativeAndExactPrecision.model: These problems involve exponentially small coordinates, multiplicative determinant error, exact integer output, or componentwise guarantees that are not captured by 1/poly(n) additive error.

polyConditionedGeneralLinearSystems.statement: For a polynomially conditioned general matrix and 1/poly(n) additive accuracy, use O(n^omega) in the dense case and O_tilde(n^{(3 omega - 4)/(omega - 1)}) in the sparse case as comparison points.

exactGeneralIntegerLinearSystems.statement: Storjohann's reduction gives essentially O_tilde(n^omega) bit complexity for exact general integer linear systems; sparsity alone does not improve this benchmark.

minPlus.statement: The conjectured n times nnz cost of min-plus product is recorded as a precision-sensitive fine-grained benchmark, not as a proved lower bound.

resolutionAudit.method: For each record, the audit fixed the graph class, error model, arithmetic model, and target bound; read the primary sources named in the record (theorem statements, not only abstracts) to extract explicit baselines; searched exact phrases plus solver, sparsifier, dynamic, counting, eigenvalue, determinant, and exact-linear-algebra synonyms; searched forward from cited anchor papers by title, authors, and citations; scanned the STOC 2026, FOCS 2026, and SODA 2026 paper lists by relevant title keywords; and checked candidate claims against primary-source abstracts, theorem statements, or conclusions. A negative search result is evidence for catalog curation, not a proof that a problem is open; unrefereed preprints are recorded as claims.

problems.sourceStatement: Solve undirected Laplacians in vector error faster than Jambulapati-Sidford '21.
problems.wordDescription:
Jambulapati and Sidford give a randomized Laplacian solver whose expected running time is linear in the number of edges up to an iterated-logarithmic factor, with logarithmic dependence on the normwise accuracy $\epsilon$. The abstract writes the overhead as $(\log\log n)^{O(1)}$, but the theorem is explicit: the SODA 2021 version proves $O(m(\log\log n)^{13+4\sqrt{10}+\chi}\log(1/\epsilon))$ for any $\chi>0$ (the authors note this exponent is below $26$ for $\chi<0.1$), and the revised arXiv v2 / ACM TALG 2024 version improves it to $O(m(\log\log n)^{6+2\sqrt{10}+\chi}\log(1/\epsilon))$, i.e. exponent about $12.32+\chi$. This replaced the earlier $O(m\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(1/\epsilon))$ bound of Cohen, Kyng, Miller, Pachocki, Peng, Rao and Xu (STOC 2014). The authors themselves state that they made only limited attempts to optimize the $\log\log n$ dependence.

The question is to beat this bound without weakening the energy-norm guarantee: a strictly smaller explicit $(\log\log n)$ exponent, removal of the iterated-logarithmic overhead down to $O(m\log(1/\epsilon))$, or a matching lower bound in a clearly specified word-RAM model would all count. Complexity is measured in operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words, so the integer weights in $[1,n^{10}]$ fit in a constant number of words; questions about the number of bits of precision needed beyond this convention, and about entrywise or exponentially small outputs, belong to the catalog's precision-sensitive problems (in particular #4). As of 2026-09-20 no published or preprint result found in our search improves the graph-size dependence of the Jambulapati-Sidford solver for this sequential, normwise task; the 2021-2026 progress located concerns parallel work/depth, entrywise bit complexity, directed/Eulerian solvers, or practical approximate Cholesky, none of which changes the baseline here.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Let $G=(V,E,w)$ be a connected undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and positive integer weights $w_e\in[1,n^{10}]$, let $L=\sum_{e=\{u,v\}}w_e(\mathbf 1_u-\mathbf 1_v)(\mathbf 1_u-\mathbf 1_v)^\top$ be its Laplacian, and let $b\in\mathbb Z^n$ be an $O(\log n)$-bit integer vector with $\mathbf 1^\top b=0$. Writing $x=L^\dagger b$ and $\|y\|_L=\sqrt{y^\top L y}$, the task is, for a given $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, to output $\tilde x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\|\tilde x-x\|_L\le\epsilon\|x\|_L$ with probability at least $2/3$ (equivalently, up to constant changes in $\epsilon$ via Markov's inequality, the expected-squared-error guarantee $\mathbb E\|\tilde x-x\|_L^2\le\epsilon\|x\|_L^2$ used by Jambulapati and Sidford; a high-probability variant costs an extra $O(\log\log n)$ factor by their remark). Running time is counted in word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words, so each weight and each entry of $b$ occupies $O(1)$ words.

The baseline is the solver of Jambulapati and Sidford (arXiv:2011.08806; SODA 2021; ACM TALG 2024), whose Theorem 1.6 gives, for graphs with polynomially bounded weights and any constant $\chi>0$, expected running time $O(m(\log\log n)^{6+2\sqrt{10}+\chi}\log(1/\epsilon))$ in the arXiv v2 / TALG version (the paper remarks $6+\sqrt{40}\approx12.324$); the SODA 2021 version proved the weaker exponent $13+4\sqrt{10}+\chi\approx25.65+\chi$, which the paper notes is less than $26$ for $\chi<0.1$. Both improve on the $O(m\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(1/\epsilon))$ bound of Cohen, Kyng, Miller, Pachocki, Peng, Rao and Xu (STOC 2014). The bound is stated in terms of arithmetic operations; the paper's floating-point/precision treatment is delegated to the analysis of the recursive preconditioning lemma in Appendix C of Peng's thesis rather than carried out for the whole algorithm, so an explicit $O(\log n)$-bit word-RAM analysis of the full solver is itself part of the target. The problem is solved by an algorithm with expected (or with-probability-$2/3$) running time $O(m(\log\log n)^{c}\log(1/\epsilon))$ word operations for some constant $c<6+2\sqrt{10}$, ideally $O(m\log(1/\epsilon))$, or by a lower bound in an explicitly stated word-RAM model showing that some iterated-logarithmic overhead is necessary.

literature.description: Gives the first nearly-linear $O(m\log^{c}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ recursive-preconditioning solver for SDD systems in the energy norm and proves that $O(\log\kappa(A)\log^{c}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ bits of precision suffice, without optimizing the exponent $c$.

literature.description: Gives a numerically stable $O(m\log^{2}n\log\log n\log(\epsilon^{-1}))$ SDD solver and observes that earlier $O(m\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$-type bounds assume arbitrary-precision arithmetic, so that in the unit-cost RAM with $O(\log n)$-bit words they incur extra logarithmic factors; this is the origin of the word-model framing of this record.

literature.description: Solves SDD systems with $m$ nonzeros to relative energy-norm error $\epsilon$ in $O(m\log^{1/2}n\log^{c}\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ time via $\ell_p$-stretch tree embeddings and preconditioning in expectation; this was the fastest sequential solver before Jambulapati-Sidford.

literature.description: The baseline: Theorem 1.6 gives an expected-time $\epsilon$-approximate Laplacian solver for polynomially weighted graphs running in $O(m(\log\log n)^{6+2\sqrt{10}+\chi}\log(1/\epsilon))$ for any $\chi>0$ in the arXiv v2 (2023) / ACM TALG 2024 version (the paper remarks $6+\sqrt{40}\approx12.324$), and in $O(m(\log\log n)^{13+4\sqrt{10}+\chi}\log(1/\epsilon))$ in the SODA 2021 version (exponent below $26$ for $\chi<0.1$), improving the $O(m\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(1/\epsilon))$ bound of Cohen et al. 2014.

problems.status: open (sharpened; Jambulapati-Sidford baseline exponent made explicit: (log log n)^{6+2 sqrt(10)+chi} in the TALG 2024 version)
problems.verificationNotes: This revision resolved the open placeholder for the hidden exponent by reading the full text of arXiv:2011.08806 in both versions (v1 of 17 Nov 2020, matching the SODA 2021 proceedings copy, and v2 of 31 Mar 2023, matching the ACM TALG 2024 journal version) together with the abstract, SODA DOI page and TALG DOI page. The paper does not merely write $O(1)$: Theorem 1.6 states the exponent explicitly. In v2/TALG it is $6+2\sqrt{10}+\chi$ for any $\chi>0$, with the remark that $6+\sqrt{40}\approx12.324$, derived from the recursion $8z+3+2\delta=z$ in the proof; in v1/SODA 2021 it is $13+4\sqrt{10}+\chi$ with the remark that the exponent is less than $26$ for $\chi<0.1$. The old guess of about $17$ matched neither version and was removed. The paper's error model was checked (expected squared energy-norm error, Definition 1.2; high-probability version at an extra $O(\log\log n)$ factor) and its precision treatment was checked (bound stated in arithmetic operations, floating-point analysis of the preconditioning lemma delegated to Appendix C of Peng's 2013 thesis), and the formulation now records both. The previous baseline of Cohen-Kyng-Miller-Pachocki-Peng-Rao-Xu (STOC 2014) was added with its DOI. Literature entries for Spielman-Teng 2006, Kelner-Orecchia-Sidford-Zhu 2013 and Ghadiri-Nguyen-Yang 2025 were re-fetched and their descriptions replaced by concrete verified statements; the 2025 entry is kept only as the source of the normwise-versus-entrywise bit-complexity distinction. Searches for 2021-2026 improvements (web search, arXiv API listing queries over Laplacian/SDD solvers, Semantic Scholar citations of arXiv:2011.08806, STOC 2026 accepted papers, FOCS 2026 and SODA 2027 accepted-paper searches) found no sequential normwise solver with a better graph-size dependence; the nearby results found were a 2023 parallel solver (arXiv:2304.14345, relevant to #13), entrywise SDDM solvers (arXiv:2504.19054 and arXiv:2511.16570, relevant to #4/#5), and the 2026 CAST approximate-Cholesky preprint (arXiv:2609.09255), which targets repeated practical solves rather than a sharper worst-case bound. Status is therefore kept open but sharpened with the explicit exponent.

resolutionAudit.assessment: The explicit exponent in the Jambulapati-Sidford theorem is verified from the full text of both arXiv versions and the published copies: $6+2\sqrt{10}+\chi$ (about $12.32+\chi$) in arXiv v2 / TALG 2024 and $13+4\sqrt{10}+\chi$ (below $26$ for $\chi<0.1$) in SODA 2021. No primary source dated 2021 through 2026-09-20 was found that improves the $m(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(1/\epsilon)$ expected word-operation bound for sequential undirected Laplacian solving in the energy norm; all located follow-ups change the objective (parallel depth/work, entrywise bit complexity, directed/Eulerian systems, practical Cholesky) rather than this bound. Confidence is high for the exponent and medium-to-high for the absence of improvements, since a very recent preprint could have been missed by keyword search.

problems.sourceStatement: Solve directed polynomial-mixing-time Laplacians in vector error faster.
problems.wordDescription:
Every known fast directed Laplacian solver runs through the Eulerian case: Cohen, Kelner, Peebles, Peng, Sidford, and Vladu reduce a strongly connected system with mixing time $t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ to $O(\log(n\, t_{\mathrm{mix}}/\epsilon))$ Eulerian solves (stated in their paper as $O(\log^2(n\kappa/\epsilon))$ solves to constant accuracy), Peng and Song solve an Eulerian system by sparsified block elimination in time $O(T_S(m)+N_S(n)\log n\log(n/\epsilon))+\tilde O(T_S(N_S(n))\log n)$ given any Eulerian sparsifier of size $N_S(n)$ built in time $T_S(m)$, and Jambulapati, Sachdeva, Sidford, Tian, and Zhao supply an $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^2 n\log^2\log n)$-edge Eulerian sparsifier in $\breve O(m\log^3 n)$ time. Together these give an Eulerian solver running in $\breve O(m\log^3 n+n\log^6 n)$ time and, through the reduction, a strongly connected polynomial-mixing solver running in $\breve O(m\log^5 n+n\log^8 n)$ time for $\epsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ (JSSTZ Corollary 43), where $\breve O$ hides $\mathrm{poly}(\log\log n)$ factors; a direct count of the reduction saves one $\log(n/\epsilon)$ factor but is not stated as a theorem anywhere.

The question is to beat these logarithmic factors for the full strongly connected polynomial-mixing problem, in the same energy-norm error model, with the cost of the reduction to Eulerian systems included. The undirected comparison point is the $O(m(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(1/\epsilon))$ solver of Jambulapati and Sidford; nothing comparable is known for directed graphs, where the polylogarithmic sparsifier size, the repeated re-sparsification inside block elimination, and the $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$ Eulerian solves of the reduction each contribute logarithmic factors. Neither Peng-Song nor Jambulapati-Sachdeva-Sidford-Tian-Zhao analyzes finite-precision arithmetic, so the word-operation bound above assumes their arithmetic is charged at $O(1)$ word operations per real operation.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Let $G$ be a strongly connected directed graph on $n$ vertices with $m$ arcs and integer arc weights in $[1,n^{10}]$, let $L=D-A^{\top}$ be its (column) directed Laplacian, and assume the lazy random walk on $G$ has mixing time $t_{\mathrm{mix}}\le n^{O(1)}$ (equivalently, by Cohen-Kelner-Peebles-Peng-Sidford-Vladu Theorem 21, $\|L^{\dagger}\|_2$ and the condition number $\kappa(L)$ are $n^{O(1)}$). Given $b\in\operatorname{im}(L)$ and $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, compute $\tilde x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\|\tilde x-L^{\dagger}b\|_{L_{U}}\le\epsilon\,\|L^{\dagger}b\|_{L_{U}}$, where $L_{U}$ is the Laplacian of the underlying undirected graph and $\|y\|_{L_U}=\sqrt{y^{\top}L_U y}$ (for Eulerian $L$ this is the $U[L]=(L+L^{\top})/2$ energy norm used by Peng-Song); the algorithm may be randomized and must succeed with probability at least $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, and running time is counted in word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words, charging the real-arithmetic operations of the cited solvers as $O(1)$ word operations each.

Baseline. Peng-Song (arXiv:2111.10257, Theorem 1.1) solve an Eulerian system in time $O(T_S(m)+N_S(n)\log n\log(n/\epsilon))+\tilde O(T_S(N_S(n))\log n)$ given a sparsifier of size $N_S(n)$ computable in time $T_S(m)$; with the Jambulapati-Sachdeva-Sidford-Tian-Zhao sparsifier (arXiv:2408.10172, Theorem 2: $T_S(m)=\breve O(m\log^3 n)$, $N_S(n)=O(n\log^2 n\log^2\log n)$ for constant $\epsilon$) this gives $\breve O(m\log^3 n+n\log^6 n)$ for Eulerian systems with $\epsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ (their Corollary 3), and the Cohen-Kelner-Peebles-Peng-Sidford-Vladu reduction (arXiv:1608.03270, Theorems 40 and 42) yields their Corollary 43 for general directed Laplacians, $\breve O\bigl(m\log^2(nU/(\delta\epsilon))\log^3(nU/\epsilon)+n\log^2(nU)\log^3(nU/(\delta\epsilon))\log^3(nU/\epsilon)\bigr)$ with failure probability $\delta$ and weight ratio $U$, i.e. $\breve O(m\log^5 n+n\log^8 n)$ under the conventions above with $\epsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, where $\breve O$ hides $\mathrm{poly}(\log\log n)$ factors. (Counting the reduction directly as $O(\log(n\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}/\epsilon))$ Eulerian solves to accuracy $\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon/n)$, as Peng-Song Section 2.4 states, gives $\breve O(m\log^2 n\log^2(n/\epsilon)+n\log^5 n\log^2(n/\epsilon))$, i.e. $\breve O(m\log^4 n+n\log^7 n)$, but no source states this as a theorem.) Target: an algorithm for the strongly connected polynomial-mixing problem above, including the cost of the reduction to Eulerian systems, running in $\breve O(m\log^{c}n+n\log^{c'}n)$ word operations for $\epsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ with $c<4$ and $c'<7$ (strictly below both the stated and the directly counted baseline), with the ultimate goal $O(m(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(n/\epsilon))$ matching the undirected bound of Jambulapati-Sidford (arXiv:2011.08806); any such result must state its normalization of $b$, its solution norm, and its success probability explicitly.

problems.verificationNotes: Fetched the arXiv abstract pages of all seven literature entries and read the full PDFs of arXiv:1608.03270 (Theorems 21, 39, 40, 42 and the definition $T_{\mathrm{solve}}=(nm^{3/4}+n^{2/3}m)\log^3 n$ as a constant-accuracy Eulerian solve), arXiv:2111.10257 (Theorem 1.1 and Section 2.4) and arXiv:2408.10172 (Theorem 2, Corollary 3, Corollary 40, Proposition 42, Corollary 43, and the definition of $\breve O$ as hiding polyloglog$(nU)$ factors). Derived the explicit exponent by substituting $T_S(m)=\breve O(m\log^3 n)$ and $N_S(n)=\breve O(n\log^2 n)$ into Peng-Song Theorem 1.1, giving $\breve O(m\log^3 n+n\log^6 n)$ for Eulerian systems (matching JSSTZ Corollary 3), and then applying the strongly-connected-to-Eulerian reduction: JSSTZ Corollary 43 (which restates CKPPSV16 Theorem 42 as $\log^2(n\kappa/\epsilon)$ Eulerian solves to accuracy $\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon/(n\kappa))$) gives $\breve O(m\log^5 n+n\log^8 n)$ for $\epsilon,\delta=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, while a direct count using CKPPSV16's structure (Theorem 40's $\log^2$ is one $\log$ of iterations times one $\log$ of refinement of a constant-accuracy solve; Peng-Song Section 2.4 states $O(\log(T_{\mathrm{mix}}/\epsilon))$ Eulerian systems) gives $\breve O(m\log^4 n+n\log^7 n)$; the record states the former as the baseline and flags the latter as derived but not stated. Replaced the exponent placeholder and the vague claim that JSSTZ 'improved the polylogarithmic factors' with these explicit bounds; corrected the reduction citation from arXiv:1611.00755 (which fetches as Cohen-Kelner-Peebles-Peng-Rao-Sidford-Vladu's almost-linear Eulerian solver, not the reduction) to arXiv:1608.03270; added arXiv:2311.06232 and the undirected comparison point arXiv:2011.08806; noted that the poly-mixing hypothesis is what makes the $\log(n\kappa)$ factors of the reduction $O(\log n)$ (Corollary 43 of JSSTZ omits $\kappa$ from its statement, and JSSTZ's Section 8 restricts to poly(n)-bounded conditioning). Searched arXiv listings and the web for 2024-2026 Eulerian/directed Laplacian solvers and sparsifiers; the only newer items found (arXiv:2507.19632 dynamic directed sparsifiers, arXiv:2509.13891 sublinear asymmetric-DD scalar estimation, arXiv:2601.08111 derandomized matrix concentration, arXiv:2609.08177 nonlinear directed Laplacian sparsification) do not improve the static full-vector bound. No change to `problem` or `sourceStatement`.

resolutionAudit.assessment: Open. The best stated bound for strongly connected polynomially mixing directed Laplacian systems in energy-norm error is JSSTZ'24 Corollary 43, $\breve O(m\log^5 n+n\log^8 n)$ for $\epsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ (Eulerian core $\breve O(m\log^3 n+n\log^6 n)$ via Peng-Song'21), and a direct count of the CKPPSV'16 reduction plausibly lowers this to $\breve O(m\log^4 n+n\log^7 n)$. No 2024-2026 result was found that gives a faster static solver for the Eulerian or the strongly connected case, and nothing approaches the undirected $O(m(\log\log n)^{O(1)}\log(1/\epsilon))$ bound. Confidence is medium rather than high because the exact exponent of the reduction overhead differs by one $\log(n/\epsilon)$ between the stated corollary and a direct count, and because finite-precision costs of the directed solvers are not analyzed in the sources.

problems.sourceStatement: Obtain a separation between solving directed Laplacians with arbitrary mixing times in vector error and solving general integer matrices in the classical high-accuracy regime, or show reductions between them.
problems.problem: Faster Directed Lx = b, arbitrary mixing time
problems.wordDescription:
Nearly-linear directed Laplacian solvers reduce a strongly connected system to polylogarithmically many Eulerian solves, but the number of solves and the accuracy they need grow with $\log\kappa$, where the condition number $\kappa$ is polynomially equivalent to the mixing time of the random walk. Integer weights in $[1,n^{10}]$ do not keep $\kappa$ polynomial (a biased walk on a directed path already has $\kappa = 2^{\Theta(n\log n)}$), and in that regime the best directed bounds, $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\,\log^{O(1)}t_{\mathrm{mix}}\,\log(1/\epsilon))$ randomized (Cohen et al. 2018) and $m^{1+o(1)}\log^{O(1)}(\kappa\epsilon^{-1})$ deterministic (Kyng, Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg 2022), become $m\cdot n^{O(1)}$ with an unspecified exponent and are not known to beat the $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ bit complexity with which Storjohann's lifting solves any nonsingular integer system exactly. Polynomial mixing is problem #2; this record asks whether directed graph structure still gives a polynomial advantage once $\log\kappa$ is polynomial in $n$, or whether the two tasks are equivalent.

Neither direction is settled as of September 2026. No algorithm exploits directed Laplacian structure with a running time that is independent of $\kappa$ and below $n^{\omega}$, and no hardness reduction targets directed Laplacians: Kyng and Zhang (2017) show that nearly-linear solvers for multi-commodity Laplacians, truss stiffness matrices or total-variation matrices would solve all polynomially conditioned integer systems, but their constructions do not produce ordinary directed Laplacians, and a reduction of general integer systems into arbitrary-mixing directed Laplacians (a larger target class than the polynomially mixing one, so formally an easier reduction to obtain) has not appeared. The vector-norm error model is essential here; the variant in which the general-matrix side must instead meet an entrywise guarantee belongs to the catalog's precision-sensitive regime and is not part of this record.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Input: the Laplacian $L = D - A^{\top} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n\times n}$ of a strongly connected directed graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs and integer arc weights in $[1,n^{10}]$ (so every entry of $L$ has $O(\log n)$ bits), together with an integer vector $b \in \operatorname{im}(L)$ with $\|b\|_\infty \le n^{O(1)}$. No promise is made on the random walk $W = A^{\top}D^{-1}$: its lazy mixing time $t_{\mathrm{mix}}$, and hence the condition number $\kappa(L) = \|L\|_2\|L^{+}\|_2$, may be as large as $2^{\Theta(n\log n)}$ (a biased walk on a directed path with weights $1$ and $n^{10}$ achieves this). Mixing time and conditioning are polynomially equivalent, $\sqrt{t_{\mathrm{mix}}} \le 16\,\|(I-W)^{+}\|_1$ and $\|(I-W)^{+}\|_1 \le 4\sqrt{n}\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}\log^{2} n$ (Lemmas 26 and 30 of Cohen, Kelner, Peebles, Peng, Sidford, Vladu, arXiv:1608.03270), so the polynomially mixing case is exactly problem #2 and this record concerns $\log\kappa$ ranging up to $\Theta(n\log n)$. Task: compute $\tilde x$ with $\|\tilde x - L^{+}b\|_2 \le n^{-c}\,\|L^{+}b\|_2$ for a fixed constant $c \ge 1$ (the guarantee of Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2208.10959; any norm within $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ distortion of $\ell_2$ is interchangeable, whereas norms whose distortion from $\ell_2$ depends on $\kappa$ are not, because converting between them costs $\mathrm{poly}(\kappa)$ in the accuracy parameter), with probability at least $1 - n^{-c}$ for randomized algorithms or deterministically. Cost is bit complexity, the classical regime of this catalog; a bound proved in exact real arithmetic counts only with a precision analysis (the directed solver papers assume exact real arithmetic and only sketch a fixed-point analysis).

Baselines. (i) General-purpose: the reduced system obtained by deleting one row and column of $L$ is a nonsingular integer matrix, so Storjohann's high-order lifting returns the exact rational solution, hence any vector-norm guarantee, in $(n^{\omega}\log\|L\|)\cdot\tilde O((\log n + \log\log\|L\|)^{2}) = \tilde O(n^{\omega})$ bit operations, Las Vegas (Storjohann, J. Complexity 2005); sparsity alone does not improve this, and the sparse benchmark $\tilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)}) = O(n^{2.2716})$ of Nie (arXiv:2111.05553) requires $\kappa = n^{O(1)}$ and is therefore unavailable here. (ii) Directed-Laplacian pipeline: Eulerian systems are solved in $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\,\log(1/\epsilon))$ time (Cohen et al., arXiv:1811.10722), now $\breve O(m\log^{3}n + n\log^{6}n)$ (Jambulapati, Sachdeva, Sidford, Tian, Zhao, arXiv:2408.10172), and a general strongly connected $L$ is handled through $\log^{O(1)}(n\kappa\epsilon^{-1})$ Eulerian solves, giving $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\,\log^{O(1)}t_{\mathrm{mix}}\,\log(1/\epsilon))$ randomized (arXiv:1811.10722) and, given an upper bound $\kappa \ge \max\{\kappa(D),\kappa(L)\}$, $m^{1+o(1)}\log^{O(1)}(\kappa\epsilon^{-1})$ deterministic (Theorem 1.2 of arXiv:2208.10959). With $\log\kappa = \Theta(n\log n)$ these bounds read $m\cdot n^{O(1)}$ with an unspecified exponent, so nothing better than $\min\{\tilde O(n^{\omega}),\ m\log^{O(1)}(n\kappa)\}$ is currently known for the task above. The problem is solved by any of the following: (a) separation: an algorithm for the task with bit complexity $O(m^{1+o(1)} + n^{\omega-\delta})$ for a constant $\delta > 0$ on every instance, with no dependence on $\kappa$ or $t_{\mathrm{mix}}$; (b) reduction: a Kyng-Zhang-style efficient reduction (arXiv:1705.02944) from solving an arbitrary nonsingular integer system $Ax = c$ with $s$ nonzeros and entries $n^{O(1)}$, either exactly or to $n^{-c}$ relative $\ell_2$ error when $\kappa(A) \le n^{O(1)}$, to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ instances of the task above with $\tilde O(s)$ arcs and $\tilde O(s)$ vertices, which would show the directed task is as hard as general integer systems; or (c) a conditional lower bound of $n^{\omega - o(1)}$ bit operations for the directed task under an explicit fine-grained hypothesis about general linear systems. (The converse reduction from the directed task to a general integer system is immediate, since $L$ is itself such a matrix.)

problems.sourceStatement: Solve undirected Laplacians to entrywise error in m polylog(n) time.
problems.wordDescription:
The seed problem is solved. Farfan, Ghadiri, and Yang (STOC 2026) give an almost-linear-time entrywise solver for grounded undirected Laplacians (SDDM matrices) with integer weights and a nonnegative right-hand side: every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$, including exponentially small escape probabilities and hitting-time quantities, is returned within a multiplicative $e^{\pm\epsilon}$ factor using $\tilde O(m\,2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})})$ bit operations (up to $\mathrm{polylog}(U\epsilon^{-1}\delta^{-1})$ factors). This improves the $\tilde O(m\sqrt{n})$ bound of Ghadiri, Nguyen, and Yang (SODA 2026), which in turn had replaced the roughly $mn^2$ bit operations needed when a normwise solver is run to exponentially small accuracy.

The sharpened question, stated explicitly in the STOC 2026 paper's conclusion, is whether the $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ overhead of the low-diameter-cover construction can be reduced to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, giving a truly near-linear $O(m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ bit-complexity solver. The record covers only fixed-point (integer) inputs: for weights given in floating point, entrywise inversion of diagonally dominant matrices is APSP-hard, so that variant is a different problem and is deliberately not part of this record.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Input: a connected undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and integer weights in $[1,n^{10}]$; a nonempty grounded set $S\subset V$; and a nonnegative integer vector $b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{V\setminus S}$ with entries at most $U=n^{10}$. Let $M=L_{V\setminus S,V\setminus S}$ be the grounded Laplacian, an invertible SDDM matrix, and $x=M^{-1}b$, which is entrywise nonnegative and encodes random-walk quantities (escape probabilities, hitting times) that can be as small as $2^{-\Omega(n)}$ even for unit weights. The task is to output $\tilde x$ with $e^{-\epsilon}x_i\le\tilde x_i\le e^{\epsilon}x_i$ for all $i$, with probability at least $1-\delta$, with cost measured in bit operations (the coordinates are exponentially small, so fixed-width word operations do not capture the cost). Grounding is essential: for the singular Laplacian $L$ itself, $L^{\dagger}b$ has coordinates of both signs and multiplicative entrywise error is not meaningful. The normwise guarantee $\|\tilde x-x\|_M\le\epsilon\|x\|_M$ of Spielman--Teng-type solvers recovers such coordinates only for $\epsilon=2^{-\Theta(n)}$, which costs about $mn^2$ bit operations.

Current baseline (Farfan--Ghadiri--Yang, STOC 2026, arXiv:2511.16570, Theorem 1.1): for any $\epsilon>(nU)^{-2^{\sqrt{\log n}}}$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, an $e^{\epsilon}$-entrywise approximation whose entries are $O(\log(nU/\epsilon))$-bit floating-point numbers is computed with $\tilde O\big(m\,2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}\log U\,\log^2(U\epsilon^{-1}\delta^{-1})\big)$ bit operations, improving the $\tilde O(m\sqrt n\,\log^2(U\epsilon^{-1}\delta^{-1}))$ bound of Ghadiri--Nguyen--Yang (SODA 2026, arXiv:2504.19054, Theorem 1.5). The problem is solved by an algorithm that, for $\epsilon=n^{-O(1)}$ and $\delta=n^{-O(1)}$, computes such an $e^{\epsilon}$-entrywise approximation with $O(m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ bit operations with high probability, i.e. replaces the $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ factor by a polylogarithmic one. Only fixed-point inputs are covered: if the matrix entries were instead given as $O(\log n)$-bit floating-point numbers, computing a constant-factor entrywise approximate inverse of a (possibly symmetric) diagonally dominant matrix is as hard as APSP (Ghadiri--Nguyen--Yang, Theorem 1.2), so the floating-point variant is a separate question outside this record.

literature.description: Spielman and Teng give the first nearly-linear randomized SDD solver, producing $y$ with $\|y-A^{\dagger}b\|_A\le\epsilon\|A^{\dagger}b\|_A$ in expected $O(m\log^{c}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ time; this normwise guarantee is the baseline whose bit cost blows up to about $mn^2$ when exponentially small coordinates must be recovered.
literature.title: Nearly-Linear Time Algorithms for Preconditioning and Solving Symmetric, Diagonally Dominant Linear Systems

literature.description: Chen, Ghadiri, Nguyen, Peng, and Yang introduce the entrywise (multiplicative) error model for escape probabilities, which can be exponentially small even on unweighted undirected graphs, and give an $\tilde O(n^3(L+\log(1/\epsilon)))$-bit-operation algorithm for weighted directed graphs with $L$-bit floating-point weights.
literature.title: Entrywise Approximate Laplacian Solving

problems.sourceStatement: Obtain a separation between solving directed Laplacians with polynomial mixing time to entrywise error and solving polynomially conditioned general matrices, or show reductions between them.
problems.wordDescription:
Random-walk quantities such as escape probabilities and hitting-time-type Green's-function coordinates are entries of $M^{-1}b$ for a grounded directed Laplacian (RDDL) matrix $M$, and they can be exponentially small even on unweighted graphs with polynomial mixing time. A normwise $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ solve, which the nearly-linear-time directed solvers of Cohen et al. (2018) deliver in $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ time, says nothing about such coordinates, whereas an entrywise $e^{\pm\epsilon}$ guarantee pins down every one of them; the price is that the output needs floating-point-style scale information and the natural cost measure becomes bit complexity. The question is whether this stronger directed task is still polynomially easier than solving a general polynomially conditioned integer system to $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ error, or whether a fine-grained reduction ties the two together.

The current frontier is asymmetric. For fixed-point (integer) inputs, Ghadiri, Nguyen and Yang (2025) solve one RDDL system entrywise in $\tilde O(mn^{1+o(1)})$ bit operations, which for sparse graphs is $n^{2+o(1)}$ and already below the $\tilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})=O(n^{2.2716})$ sparse general-system bound of Nie (2021), but for dense graphs is $n^{3+o(1)}$, above the $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ dense benchmark; they leave even an $\tilde O(mn)$ algorithm for the directed case as an explicit open question. For the symmetric special case (SDDM systems), Farfan, Ghadiri and Yang (2025) obtain entrywise solutions in $\tilde O(mn^{o(1)})$ time, so directedness is now the isolated obstacle. Under floating-point inputs, the same authors show that entrywise RDDL inversion is APSP-hard, but this barrier concerns the full inverse with floating-point entries and does not apply to the integer-weight, single-right-hand-side formulation here. No reduction in either direction between the directed entrywise task and general polynomially conditioned solving is known.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Directed entrywise task. The input is a strongly connected directed graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $|V|=n$, $|E|=m$, integer arc weights $w_e\in[1,n^{10}]$, and whose random walk has mixing time $t_{\mathrm{mix}}=n^{O(1)}$; together with a nonempty proper grounded set $S\subsetneq V$ and a right-hand side $b\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{V\setminus S}\setminus\{0\}$ with $O(\log n)$-bit entries. Let $L=D-A^{\top}$ be the directed Laplacian ($D$ the diagonal of weighted out-degrees, $A$ the weighted adjacency matrix) and let $M=L_{V\setminus S,V\setminus S}$ be the grounded matrix, an invertible row-diagonally-dominant $L$-matrix (RDDL: nonpositive off-diagonal entries, nonnegative row sums) whose inverse is entrywise nonnegative; the exact solution is $x^{\star}=M^{-1}b\ge 0$, whose coordinates are escape-probability-type quantities that may be as small as $2^{-\Omega(n)}$ even when $t_{\mathrm{mix}}=n^{O(1)}$. Given $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, output $\tilde x$ with $e^{-\epsilon}x^{\star}_i\le\tilde x_i\le e^{\epsilon}x^{\star}_i$ for every $i$ with $x^{\star}_i>0$ and $\tilde x_i=0$ whenever $x^{\star}_i=0$, each $\tilde x_i$ returned as an $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$-bit floating-point number, with success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for a fixed constant $c$. Cost is measured in bit operations (bit complexity), suppressing $\mathrm{polylog}(n/\epsilon)$ factors. The best verified baseline is Theorem 1.3 of Ghadiri, Nguyen and Yang (arXiv:2504.19054): for an RDDL matrix with $m$ nonzeros, entries in $[-U,U]$ and condition number $\kappa$, $\tilde O((m+n^{1+o(1)})\,T\,\log^{O(1)}(U\kappa\epsilon^{-1}\delta^{-1}))$ bit operations return an entrywise $e^{\pm\epsilon}$ approximation of all coordinates with $x^{\star}_i\ge(nU)^{-(T+1)}\|b\|_1$, and $T=n$ gives the full entrywise solve in $\tilde O(mn^{1+o(1)})$ bit operations; the normwise directed solver of Cohen et al. (arXiv:1811.10722) runs in $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ time but only controls $\|\tilde x-x^{\star}\|$ in norm, not exponentially small coordinates.

General comparison task. Given a nonsingular integer matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{n\times n}$ with $\mathrm{nnz}(A)=m$, entries of magnitude $n^{O(1)}$ and condition number $\kappa(A)=n^{O(1)}$, and $b\in\mathbb{Z}^n$ with $O(\log n)$-bit entries, return $\tilde x$ with $\|\tilde x-A^{-1}b\|_2\le n^{-O(1)}\|A^{-1}b\|_2$; the benchmarks are $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ bit complexity in the dense case (Peng and Vempala, arXiv:2007.10254) and $\tilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})=O(n^{2.2716})$ time for $m=\tilde O(n)$ (Nie, arXiv:2111.05553). The problem is resolved by either (i) a reduction: a randomized reduction that maps an instance of one task to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ instances of the other while preserving dimension, sparsity and conditioning up to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factors (in particular, showing that entrywise directed solving with polynomial mixing time is at least as hard as general polynomially conditioned solving, or conversely that it reduces to it with no polynomial loss); or (ii) a separation: an algorithm for the directed entrywise task with bit complexity polynomially below the general benchmark at every density, e.g. $\tilde O(mn^{o(1)})$ or at least $\tilde O(mn^{1-c})$ for a constant $c>0$ together with $n^{\omega-c}$ in the dense regime, or a fine-grained lower bound (conditional on a standard hypothesis) showing the directed entrywise task cannot be solved faster than general polynomially conditioned systems. Currently the sparse regime exhibits only an upper-bound gap ($n^{2+o(1)}$ versus $n^{2.2716}$) and the dense regime has the directed bound $n^{3+o(1)}$ above $n^{\omega}$; neither a reduction nor a separation in the above sense is known.

problems.sourceStatement: Give a faster algorithm for finding an O(n)-sized cut or spectral sparsifier for undirected Laplacians.
problems.wordDescription:
For constant accuracy, $O(n)$-edge spectral (hence cut) sparsifiers exist by Batson, Spielman and Srivastava, and they can now be built in nearly-linear randomized time: Lee and Sun (2017) obtained $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $\tilde O(m\,\epsilon^{-O(1)})$ time, and Jambulapati, Reis and Tian (2023) sharpened the runtime to $\tilde O(m\,\epsilon^{-3.5})$. Since the catalog suppresses polylogarithmic factors for this problem, the seed milestone of "$O(n)$ edges in nearly-linear time" is achieved, and the record now asks for the remaining polynomial-factor and model-level improvements: reducing the $\epsilon$-dependence of the runtime toward the output-size limit $\tilde O(m + n\epsilon^{-2})$, and giving a deterministic construction of comparable speed and size. On the deterministic side the only polynomial-time route to optimal size is the original Batson-Spielman-Srivastava barrier method, and the 2026 Li-Vaughn algorithm reaches $m^{1+o(1)} + \tilde O_\epsilon(n^2)$ time only with $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^{24+o(1)} n)$ edges, so it neither matches the optimal size nor is almost-linear on sparse graphs.

The seed statement deliberately allows the weaker cut guarantee, but every known $O(n/\epsilon^2)$-edge cut sparsifier is obtained through spectral sparsification; combinatorial cut-sparsification methods reach $O(n\log n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $O(m\cdot\min(\alpha(n)\log(m/n),\log n))$ time (Forster and de Vos) and $O(n\log^2 n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $O(m)$ time for polynomially weighted graphs (Fung, Hariharan, Harvey and Panigrahi), so an $O(n)$-edge cut sparsifier in genuinely linear time would be new even without any spectral guarantee. The size $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ is optimal up to constants, since any data structure encoding all cut values to within $1\pm\epsilon$ needs $\Omega(n\log n/\epsilon^2)$ bits (Carlson, Kolla, Srivastava and Trevisan). No 2024-2026 result changes the randomized runtime frontier; the only recent movement is deterministic.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Input: a connected undirected graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and integer weights $w_e \in [1,n^{10}]$, together with an accuracy parameter $\epsilon \in (0,1/2]$ (constant $\epsilon$ is the primary case). Output: a reweighted subgraph $H=(V,F,\tilde w)$ with $|F| = O(n/\epsilon^2)$ that is either a spectral sparsifier, $(1-\epsilon)\,x^\top L_G x \le x^\top L_H x \le (1+\epsilon)\,x^\top L_G x$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^V$, or, in the weaker cut version, satisfies the same inequality for all $x \in \{0,1\}^V$. Randomized algorithms must succeed with probability at least $1 - 1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$; running time is counted in word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words, with polylogarithmic factors suppressed as for the other problems in this regime, and the output size must be exactly the stated $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ (no hidden $\log n$ or $\epsilon^{-O(1)}$ blow-up). Size $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ is optimal up to constants, since $\Omega(n\log n/\epsilon^2)$ bits are necessary to encode all cut values to within $1\pm\epsilon$ (Carlson-Kolla-Srivastava-Trevisan, arXiv:1712.10261).

Baselines. Randomized: Lee-Sun (arXiv:1702.08415) give $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $\tilde O(m\,\epsilon^{-O(1)})$ time (stated as $\tilde O(m\,\epsilon^{-6.5})$ by later work), and Jambulapati-Reis-Tian (arXiv:2305.08434) improve this to $\tilde O(m\,\epsilon^{-3.5})$; effective-resistance sampling (Spielman-Srivastava, arXiv:0803.0929) gives only $O(n\log n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in nearly-linear time. Deterministic: Batson-Spielman-Srivastava (arXiv:0808.0163) give $\lceil d(n-1)\rceil$ edges with approximation ratio $(d+1+2\sqrt d)/(d+1-2\sqrt d)$ in polynomial time, and Li-Vaughn (arXiv:2608.13910) give $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^{24+o(1)} n)$ edges in $m^{1+o(1)} + O(n^2 \epsilon^{-9/2}\log^{113/2+o(1)} n)$ time. Cut-only: $O(n\log n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $O(m\cdot\min(\alpha(n)\log(m/n),\log n))$ time (Forster-de Vos, arXiv:2112.03120) and $O(n\log^2 n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $O(m)$ time for polynomial weights (Fung-Hariharan-Harvey-Panigrahi, arXiv:1004.4080). Targets that would count as progress on the sharpened problem: (a) a randomized algorithm with $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ edges running in $\tilde O(m\,\epsilon^{-c})$ time for some $c < 3.5$, with $\tilde O(m + n\epsilon^{-2})$ as the natural limit; (b) a deterministic algorithm with $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ edges in $\tilde O(m)$ or $m^{1+o(1)}$ time on all graphs, i.e. without the $\tilde O(n^2)$ additive term and $\log^{24+o(1)} n$ size overhead of Li-Vaughn; (c) as the strongest form, an $O(n)$-edge cut or spectral sparsifier for constant $\epsilon$ in $O(m)$ expected word operations, a polylogarithmic-factor question that lies outside this record's default regime but is recorded because it is the literal reading of the seed statement.

problems.sourceStatement: Obtain the smallest possible Eulerian spectral sparsifier
problems.wordDescription:
Eulerian sparsification asks for a reweighted subgraph of a directed Eulerian graph that stays Eulerian and approximates the asymmetric directed Laplacian in the norm induced by the underlying undirected Laplacian, the notion introduced by Cohen, Kelner, Peebles, Peng, Rao, Sidford and Vladu in 2016. Because it generalizes undirected spectral sparsification, the undirected $\Omega(n/\epsilon^2)$ edge lower bound carries over, whereas undirected graphs achieve $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ edges by Batson, Spielman and Srivastava. Every known Eulerian construction still pays extra logarithmic factors: Sachdeva, Thudi and Zhao (2023) gave $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^2 n\log^2\log n + n\epsilon^{-4/3}\log^{8/3} n)$ arcs existentially via short-cycle decompositions and the Bansal-Jiang-Meka partial matrix Spencer result, and Jambulapati, Sachdeva, Sidford, Tian and Zhao (2024) gave $O(\min\{n\epsilon^{-2}\log n + n\epsilon^{-4/3}\log^{5/3} n,\; n\epsilon^{-2}\log^{3/2} n\})$ arcs in polynomial time and $\breve O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^2 n)$ arcs in $\breve O(m\log^3 n)$ time, which also drives the fastest known Eulerian Laplacian solver.

The question is whether directionality plus exact degree balance genuinely costs extra arcs or whether the undirected optimum $\Theta(n/\epsilon^2)$ is attainable, first existentially and then by an almost-linear-time algorithm. The 2024 paper isolates a concrete discrepancy obstacle: a partial-coloring form of matrix Spencer under a variance normalization would already remove the $\epsilon^{-4/3}$ term and give $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log n)$ arcs. The matrix Spencer conjecture itself (operator-norm-one matrices, $O(\sqrt n)$ discrepancy) was announced proved by Akbas and Sra in August 2026, with follow-up expositions and alternative proofs in September 2026, but as of 2026-09-20 no source has translated this into a new Eulerian sparsity bound, and a 2025 fully dynamic construction by Zhao keeps $O(\epsilon^{-2}n\,\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ size, so the static size gap remains open.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Input: a strongly connected Eulerian directed graph $\vec G=(V,E,w)$ with $|V|=n$, $|E|=m$, integer weights $w_e\in[1,n^{10}]$ (so weighted in-degree equals weighted out-degree at every vertex), directed Laplacian $\vec L_{\vec G}=D_{\mathrm{out}}-A^{\top}$, and undirected Laplacian $L_G=\tfrac12(\vec L_{\vec G}+\vec L_{\vec G}^{\top})$ of the underlying undirected graph. For $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, an $\epsilon$-approximate Eulerian sparsifier is a reweighted subgraph $\vec H=(V,E_H,w_H)$ with $E_H\subseteq E$, $w_H>0$, $\vec H$ Eulerian, and $\|L_G^{\dagger/2}(\vec L_{\vec G}-\vec L_{\vec H})L_G^{\dagger/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\epsilon$ (the standard asymmetric approximation notion of Cohen, Kelner, Peebles, Peng, Rao, Sidford, and Vladu). Let $s(n,\epsilon)$ be the smallest $s$ such that every such $\vec G$ admits an $\epsilon$-approximate Eulerian sparsifier with $|E_H|\le s$. Since undirected graphs are Eulerian and the notion reduces to undirected spectral approximation on them, $s(n,\epsilon)=\Omega(n/\epsilon^2)$, while Batson, Spielman, and Srivastava show the undirected analogue is $O(n/\epsilon^2)$.

Baselines (Jambulapati, Sachdeva, Sidford, Tian, and Zhao, arXiv:2408.10172): existential/polynomial time $s(n,\epsilon)=O(\min\{n\epsilon^{-2}\log n+n\epsilon^{-4/3}\log^{5/3}n,\;n\epsilon^{-2}\log^{3/2}n\})$; algorithmic $\breve O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^2 n)$ arcs computed with high probability in $\breve O(m\log^3 n)$ word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words, where $\breve O$ hides $\mathrm{polyloglog}(n)$ factors. Target: prove or refute $s(n,\epsilon)=\Theta(n/\epsilon^2)$; the existential question counts as solved by an $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ upper bound (or by a lower bound of $\omega(n/\epsilon^2)$ on some Eulerian family), and the algorithmic question by a randomized (success probability $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$) or deterministic $m^{1+o(1)}$-time construction with $O(n/\epsilon^2)$ arcs. Intermediate progress of interest: $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log n)$ arcs, which the 2024 paper shows would follow from a variance-normalized partial-coloring matrix Spencer statement (its Conjecture 60).

problems.sourceStatement: Improve max(update,query) time for fully dynamic approximate effective resistance on general weighted graphs.
problems.problem: Faster undirected weighted dynamic effective resistances
problems.wordDescription:
Effective resistance is a basic measure of connectivity and a central primitive behind spectral sparsification, electrical-flow optimization, and random-walk analysis. Maintaining a $(1\pm\epsilon)$ spectral edge sparsifier under updates costs only polylogarithmic time (Abraham, Durfee, Koutis, Krinninger, Peng 2016), but a sparsifier alone does not answer an arbitrary $(s,t)$ resistance query quickly: evaluating $(e_s-e_t)^\top L^\dagger (e_s-e_t)$ still requires access to an inverse or to a dynamically maintained Schur complement onto a terminal set containing $s$ and $t$, and rebuilding a static resistance oracle on the sparsifier after every update costs $\tilde O(n\,\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon))$ per update.

For general weighted graphs, the fully dynamic frontier is the random-walk Schur-complement line: $\tilde O(m^{4/5}\epsilon^{-4})$ (Durfee, Gao, Goranci, Peng 2018, unweighted), $\tilde O(n^{5/6}\epsilon^{-6})$ (Durfee, Gao, Goranci, Sachdeva 2019, weighted), and $\tilde O(n^{2/3+o(1)}\epsilon^{-O(1)})$ amortized update and query time against an oblivious adversary (Chen, Goranci, Henzinger, Peng, Saranurak 2020), which has not been improved since. Against an adaptive adversary the best fully dynamic bound is $n^{3/4+o(1)}$ amortized (Beimel, Kaplan, Mansour, Nissim, Saranurak, Stemmer 2021). In the partially dynamic (insertions-only or deletions-only) setting, Goranci, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg, Zhao, Zoecklein (2026) obtain $\tilde O(n^2/\epsilon^7)$ total update time with $\tilde O(1/\epsilon^2)$ worst-case query time against an adaptive adversary, which is near-optimal for dense monotone sequences but does not address the fully dynamic case. The only known conditional lower bounds (Goranci, Henzinger, Peng 2018, via OMv) concern exact or very-high-accuracy $s$-$t$ resistance and say nothing about constant-factor approximation, so the gap between polylogarithmic and $n^{2/3}$ per-operation cost is wide open.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Let $G=(V,E,w)$ be a connected undirected graph on $n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges at any time and integer conductances $w_e\in[1,n^{10}]$, undergoing an online, intermixed sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions, and conductance changes that keep $G$ connected, interleaved with queries. Let $L$ be the weighted Laplacian and $R_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,t)=(e_s-e_t)^\top L^{\dagger}(e_s-e_t)$. On a query $(s,t)$ the data structure must return $\tilde R$ with $(1-\epsilon)R_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,t)\le \tilde R\le(1+\epsilon)R_{\mathrm{eff}}(s,t)$ for a fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1)$; all answers over a polynomially long operation sequence must be correct with probability at least $1-n^{-c}$. Time is measured in word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words (bit complexity is acceptable), polylogarithmic factors in $n$ and polynomial factors in $1/\epsilon$ are suppressed, and the cost of an algorithm is $\max(\text{amortized update time},\text{query time})$. The adversary model must be stated: oblivious (the update sequence is fixed in advance and independent of the algorithm's randomness) or adaptive (updates may depend on previous answers).

Baseline. Against an oblivious adversary, Chen, Goranci, Henzinger, Peng, Saranurak (arXiv:2005.02368, Theorem 8.1) achieve $\tilde O(n^{2/3+o(1)}\epsilon^{-O(1)})$ amortized update and query time for general weighted graphs, improving the earlier $\tilde O(n^{5/6}\epsilon^{-6})$ weighted bound of Durfee, Gao, Goranci, Sachdeva (arXiv:1906.10530) and the $\tilde O(m^{4/5}\epsilon^{-4})$ unweighted bound of Durfee, Gao, Goranci, Peng (arXiv:1804.04038). Against an adaptive adversary the best bound is $n^{3/4+o(1)}$ amortized (Beimel, Kaplan, Mansour, Nissim, Saranurak, Stemmer, arXiv:2111.03980, Theorem 1.2), and the naive alternative of resampling a $(1\pm\epsilon)$ spectral sparsifier and rebuilding a static oracle costs $\tilde O(n\,\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon))$ per update. If only insertions or only deletions occur, Goranci, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg, Zhao, Zoecklein (arXiv:2608.26037, Theorem 1.1) give $\tilde O(n^2/\epsilon^7)$ total update time and $\tilde O(1/\epsilon^2)$ worst-case query time against an adaptive adversary, i.e. $\tilde O(n^2/m)$ amortized per update, which beats $n^{2/3}$ only when $m\ge n^{4/3+\Omega(1)}$. The only conditional lower bound, from the OMv conjecture (Goranci, Henzinger, Peng, arXiv:1802.09111, Theorem 1.4), rules out $O(n^{1-\delta})$ worst-case update with $O(n^{2-\delta})$ query time for exact (or sufficiently high-accuracy) $s$-$t$ resistance even in the incremental or decremental setting, and gives no obstruction for constant $\epsilon$. Target. Give a fully dynamic data structure for general weighted graphs with $\max(\text{amortized update},\text{query})=O(n^{2/3-\delta})$ for some constant $\delta>0$ against an oblivious adversary, or $O(n^{3/4-\delta})$ against an adaptive adversary, or improve the amortized bounds to worst-case; alternatively prove a conditional lower bound of $n^{\Omega(1)}$ per operation for $(1\pm\epsilon)$-approximate queries with constant $\epsilon$. The problem is closed when both update and query cost $\mathrm{poly}(\log n,1/\epsilon)$, or when matching conditional upper and lower bounds are known up to $n^{o(1)}$ factors.

problems.sourceStatement: Give a faster data structure for returning all edges whose electrical energy exceed \epsilon fraction of the total energy in electrical flows, under updates to resistances and demands.
problems.wordDescription:
Interior-point and multiplicative-weights methods built on electrical flows typically need only the few edges that carry an $\epsilon$ fraction of the current energy, yet recomputing the full flow after each resistance or demand change costs nearly linear time per step. Gao, Liu, and Peng (2021) and then van den Brand, Gao, Jambulapati, Lee, Liu, Peng, and Sidford (2021) built exactly such heavy-hitter oracles from dynamic spectral vertex sparsifiers and used them for the first sparse max-flow algorithms faster than Goldberg-Rao, at $\tilde O(m^{3/2-1/328}\log U)$ and $\tilde O(m^{3/2-1/58}\log U)$ respectively. The stronger 2021 locator handles single-coordinate changes to conductances and to an edge vector encoding the demand in $\tilde O(\beta^{-2}\epsilon^{-2})$ time each and returns $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ candidate edges in $\tilde O(\beta m\epsilon^{-2})$ time, but only against an oblivious adversary, only for $O(\beta m)$ updates before a rebuild, and only with a threshold measured against an upper bound on the energy rather than the energy itself; balancing the parameters gives roughly $\tilde O(m^{3/4})$ amortized per operation.

The open problem is to beat these restricted bounds with a reusable oracle: general demands and resistance updates (ideally also edge insertions and deletions), a threshold relative to the true energy with an $\epsilon/2$ exclusion gap and estimates of the reported currents, amortized update and query time $m^{3/4-\Omega(1)}$ against an oblivious adversary or $m^{15/16-\Omega(1)}$ against an adaptive one, and no bounded-update-count assumption beyond periodic rebuilding. Alternatively, prove a lower bound; the only conditional lower bounds nearby are the OMv-based bounds of Goranci, Henzinger, and Peng for exact dynamic effective resistance, which say nothing about constant-$\epsilon$ heavy hitters. The record is closed once upper and lower bounds match up to polylogarithmic factors. Since almost-linear-time max-flow (Chen et al. 2022) now uses min-ratio cycles instead of electrical flows, the question stands on its own as a dynamic-algorithms problem rather than as a route to faster flow.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Input: a connected undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and integer resistances $r_e\in[1,n^{10}]$ (conductances $w_e=1/r_e$); write $B\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times V}$ for the signed incidence matrix, $R=\mathrm{diag}(r)$, $L=B^{\top}R^{-1}B$, and let $b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}$ be a zero-sum demand. The electrical flow is $f=R^{-1}BL^{\dagger}b$, its energy is $\mathcal{E}=f^{\top}Rf=b^{\top}L^{\dagger}b=\|R^{1/2}f\|_2^2$, and the energy of edge $e$ is $r_ef_e^2=(R^{1/2}f)_e^2$. A dynamic electrical-flow heavy-hitter oracle must support (i) $\textsc{UpdateR}(e,r')$: set $r_e\leftarrow r'\in[1,n^{10}]$ (the sharpened problem also asks for edge insertions and deletions, which the known constructions do not support beyond setting a conductance of a fixed edge set to zero); (ii) $\textsc{UpdateB}(u,v,\delta)$: $b\leftarrow b+\delta(\chi_u-\chi_v)$, so arbitrary zero-sum demands can be built from sparse changes; and (iii) $\textsc{Locate}(\epsilon)$: return a set $H\subseteq E$ containing every edge with $r_ef_e^2\ge\epsilon^2\mathcal{E}$ and no edge with $r_ef_e^2<\epsilon^2\mathcal{E}/4$ (equivalently $\sqrt{r_e}|f_e|\ge\epsilon\sqrt{\mathcal{E}}$ versus $\sqrt{r_e}|f_e|<(\epsilon/2)\sqrt{\mathcal{E}}$, which forces $|H|\le 4\epsilon^{-2}$), together with estimates $\tilde f_e$, $e\in H$, satisfying $\sqrt{r_e}|\tilde f_e-f_e|\le(\epsilon/2)\sqrt{\mathcal{E}}$. All answers over a sequence of $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ operations must be correct with probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for a constant $c\ge 1$; the default adversary is oblivious (the update sequence is fixed in advance and independent of the data structure's randomness), and the adaptive-adversary version is a stronger variant. Running times are amortized word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words with polylogarithmic factors suppressed; the trivial baseline recomputes $f$ with a nearly-linear-time Laplacian solver in $\tilde O(m\log(1/\epsilon))$ per query and $O(1)$ per update.

Verified baselines (both against oblivious adversaries, both valid only for $O(\beta m)$ updates before a rebuild). Gao, Liu, and Peng (arXiv:2101.07233), for a unit $s$-$t$ demand and parameters $0<\delta<\beta<\epsilon<1$, give a $\textsc{Locator}$ with initialization $\tilde O(m\beta^{-4}\delta^{-2}\epsilon^{-2})$, amortized resistance update $\tilde O(\delta m\epsilon^{-3}+\delta^{-2}\beta^{-6}\epsilon^{-2})$, and $\textsc{Locate}$ in $\tilde O(\beta m\epsilon^{-2})$ returning $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ edges that contain every edge of energy at least $\epsilon^2\mathcal{E}/10$, where $\mathcal{E}$ is a fixed upper bound on the energy; their single-edge $\textsc{Checker}$ (accept energy $\ge\epsilon^2\mathcal{E}$, reject energy $\le\epsilon^2\mathcal{E}/2$, return an approximate current) has amortized update time $\tilde O(\beta^{-2}\epsilon^{-2})$ and check time $\tilde O(\beta m\epsilon^{-2})$ when no temporary updates are pending. van den Brand, Gao, Jambulapati, Lee, Liu, Peng, and Sidford (arXiv:2112.00722) give, for dynamic conductances $\bar w\ge 0$, a dynamic edge vector $\bar v$ (so $b=B^{\top}\bar W^{1/2}\bar v$, which covers every zero-sum demand, and $R^{1/2}f=\Pi_{\bar w}\bar v$), and $\beta<\epsilon^2<1$, a $\textsc{Locator}$ with $\tilde O(m\beta^{-2}\epsilon^{-2})$ initialization, $\tilde O(\beta^{-2}\epsilon^{-2})$ per single-coordinate update, and $\tilde O(\beta m\epsilon^{-2})$ per $\textsc{Locate}$, returning $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ edges containing every $e$ with $|(\Pi_{\bar w}\bar v)_e|\ge\epsilon\|\bar v\|_2$, together with an $\textsc{Evaluator}$ of the same cost; since $\|\bar v\|_2\ge\sqrt{\mathcal{E}}$, the threshold is relative to an upper bound on the energy rather than the energy itself. Rebuilding every $\Theta(\beta m)$ updates with $\beta=m^{-1/4}$ gives amortized $\tilde O(m^{3/4}\epsilon^{-2})$ per operation (a derivation, not a stated theorem). The same paper's Gaussian-mechanism reduction to adaptive adversaries costs $\tilde O(m^{15/16}\epsilon^{-7/8})$ amortized per interior-point step for that method's update pattern.

Target: (a) a data structure for the model above (true-energy threshold, general demands and resistance updates, preferably also edge insertions and deletions) with amortized $\max(\text{update},\text{query})$ time $m^{3/4-\Omega(1)}\,\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1})$ against an oblivious adversary, or $m^{15/16-\Omega(1)}\,\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1})$ against an adaptive one, with no bounded-update-count restriction beyond rebuilding accounted for in the amortization; or (b) a lower bound, conditional (e.g. on OMv or SETH) or unconditional in the cell-probe model, showing $\max(\text{update},\text{query})\ge m^{c-o(1)}$ for constant $\epsilon$. The problem is closed once the best upper and lower bounds agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The only nearby conditional lower bounds (Goranci, Henzinger, and Peng, ESA 2018) concern exact or $(1+n^{-\Theta(1)})$-approximate $s$-$t$ effective resistance and do not apply to constant-$\epsilon$ heavy-hitter detection.

problems.sourceStatement: Estimate an undirected Laplacian cofactor multiplicatively (e.g. to within a factor of 2) in nearly input-linear time.
problems.wordDescription:
By the matrix-tree theorem, any cofactor of an undirected graph Laplacian equals the total weight of the graph's spanning trees, so estimating $\det(L_{-r,-r})$ is the same as approximately counting (weighted) spanning trees. The catch is scale: $\log\tau(G)$ is of order $n\log n$, so a $(1\pm\epsilon)$ estimate of the determinant is an additive-$\epsilon$ estimate of a quantity of size about $n$. Additive $\epsilon n$ error in $\log\det$ (a factor $e^{\pm\epsilon n}$ in the determinant) has been achievable in near-linear time since Hunter, El Alaoui and Bayen (2014); the genuinely multiplicative guarantee is the open question.

Durfee, Peebles, Peng and Rao (FOCS 2017) gave the first sub-matrix-multiplication estimator, $\tilde O(n^2\epsilon^{-2})$, via determinant-preserving sparsifiers with about $n^{3/2}$ edges; Chu et al. (FOCS 2018) reached $m^{1+o(1)}+n^{15/8+o(1)}\epsilon^{-7/4}$ by speeding up the effective-resistance step; Li and Sachdeva (SODA 2023) reached $\tilde O(m+n^{3/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ on expanders; and Liu, Peng and Yang (FOCS 2026) obtained $\tilde O(m^{3/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ for all graphs by repeatedly deleting uncorrelated edge sets found through electrical-flow localization, avoiding sparsifiers altogether. A September 2026 preprint of Li and Yang (arXiv:2609.03574, not yet refereed) claims $\tilde O(m+n^{3/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ on all graphs via $\ell_1$-regularized resistances, which would match the size of the best known determinant sparsifiers. Whether the $n^{3/2}$ term can be beaten on sparse graphs, let alone reduced to $m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, is open, and no hardness result is known.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Input: a connected undirected graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and integer weights $w_e\in[1,n^{10}]$, with Laplacian $L$. Fix any root $r\in V$ and let $\tau(G)=\det(L_{-r,-r})=\sum_{T}\prod_{e\in T}w_e$ (sum over spanning trees; by the matrix-tree theorem this is independent of $r$ and equals $\tfrac1n\prod_{i\ge2}\lambda_i(L)$). Given $\epsilon\in[n^{-O(1)},1/2]$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, output $\tilde\tau$ with $(1-\epsilon)\tau(G)\le\tilde\tau\le(1+\epsilon)\tau(G)$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. The error is multiplicative in $\tau(G)$, equivalently additive $O(\epsilon)$ in $\log\tau(G)$, a quantity of order $n\log n$; this is strictly stronger than the guarantee $|z-\tfrac1n\log\det A|\le\epsilon$ of Hunter, El Alaoui and Bayen, which allows a factor $e^{\pm\epsilon n}$ in the determinant and is attainable in $\tilde O(m\epsilon^{-2}\log^3 n\log^2(\kappa/\epsilon)\log(1/\delta))$ time. Cost is bit complexity (polylogarithmic factors suppressed); since $\tau(G)$ has $\Theta(n\log n)$ bits, $\tilde\tau$ is returned as $\log\tilde\tau$ to additive error $\epsilon$ or as an $O(\log n)$-bit-mantissa floating-point number.

Baselines: exact computation costs $O(n^\omega)$ arithmetic operations via Kirchhoff; $\tilde O(n^2\epsilon^{-2})$ (Durfee, Peebles, Peng, Rao, FOCS 2017), $m^{1+o(1)}+n^{15/8+o(1)}\epsilon^{-7/4}$ (Chu, Gao, Peng, Sachdeva, Sawlani, Wang, FOCS 2018), and $\tilde O(m^{3/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ with high probability (Liu, Peng, Yang, FOCS 2026), the fastest refereed bound on sparse graphs. On graphs of constant expansion, $\tilde O(m+n^{3/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ (Li, Sachdeva, SODA 2023); the unrefereed preprint arXiv:2609.03574v3 (Li, Yang, September 2026) claims the same $\tilde O(m+n^{3/2}\epsilon^{-1})$ expected time on all graphs with polynomially bounded weights and success probability $2/3$, which would make $n^{3/2}$ the bottleneck for every $m$. The target is $\tilde O(m\,\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1})\log(1/\delta))$ bit operations; a sharpened intermediate goal is $m^{1+o(1)}+n^{3/2-c}\,\mathrm{poly}(\epsilon^{-1})$ for some constant $c>0$, which would have to leave the determinant-sparsifier framework, whose known constructions need $\Omega(n^{3/2})$ edges even for random subgraphs of $K_n$. No conditional lower bound for the multiplicative problem is known.

problems.sourceStatement: Give a faster algorithm for computing a 2-approximation of det(L_{-}) for a poly mixing unit weighted L with O(n) edges, or show conditional hardness.
problems.wordDescription:
A cofactor of a directed Laplacian is, by the directed matrix-tree theorem, the total weight of spanning arborescences rooted at the deleted vertex, so a multiplicative estimate of $\det(L_{-r,-r})$ is an approximate arborescence count. The matrix is asymmetric, and the notions of approximation used by directed Laplacian solvers and Eulerian sparsifiers control a norm induced by a symmetrization rather than the determinant, so the Eulerian solvers of Cohen et al. that run in $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ time have no known counting counterpart. In the undirected case, determinant-preserving sparsification gives a $(1\pm\delta)$-approximation of any SDDM determinant in about $n^{2}\delta^{-2}$ time (Durfee-Peebles-Peng-Rao) and $\tilde O(m^{1.5}\epsilon^{-1})$ time (Liu-Peng-Yang); no directed analogue of either result was found in the literature through 2026-09-20.

Consequently the best verified way to 2-approximate the cofactor of a polynomially mixing, unit-weighted directed Laplacian with $O(n)$ arcs is to compute it exactly with generic integer-determinant algorithms: $\tilde O(n^{\omega}\log\|A\|)$ bit operations via Storjohann's shifted number system, which is $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ here because the entries are out-degrees, or $\tilde O(n^{2.66})$ bit operations via the sparse black-box method of Eberly et al. when only classical matrix multiplication is used. The question is whether the directed spectral toolkit, or the polynomial mixing time and sparsity of the input, can be exploited to beat this by a polynomial factor, ideally reaching nearly linear time, or whether a fine-grained reduction shows that even a 2-approximation in this restricted class is as hard as general integer determinants.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Let $G$ be a strongly connected directed graph with $n$ vertices, $m=O(n)$ arcs, and unit arc weights, whose random walk has polynomially bounded mixing time (the general catalog convention of integer weights in $[1,n^{10}]$ is specialized to unit weights here, following the source statement). Let $L$ be its directed Laplacian (either $D_{\mathrm{in}}-A^{\top}$ or $D_{\mathrm{out}}-A$, with $A$ the arc-adjacency matrix), fix a root $r$, and let $\tau_r=\det(L_{-r,-r})$, the determinant of the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ principal submatrix obtained by deleting row and column $r$; by Tutte's directed matrix-tree theorem $\tau_r$ equals the number of spanning arborescences of $G$ rooted at $r$, incoming or outgoing according to the convention, a positive integer with $O(n\log n)$ bits. The task is to output $\hat\tau$ with $\tau_r/2\le\hat\tau\le 2\tau_r$ with probability at least $1/2$. Because $\tau_r$ is exponentially large and a multiplicative error is required, this problem is in the catalog's exact/multiplicative precision regime and running times are measured in bit operations; word-operation bounds on $O(\log n)$-bit words may be reported when the algorithm's numbers fit in such words.

Baseline: no directed-Laplacian-specific approximation algorithm is known, so the current best is exact computation of the integer determinant. Storjohann's shifted number system (J. Complexity 2005) computes $\det(A)$ for $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{n\times n}$ in $(n^{\omega}\log\|A\|)\cdot\tilde O((\log n)^{3}+(\log\log\|A\|)^{2})$ expected bit operations (Las Vegas, under its stated cost-model assumption), which is $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ for $L_{-r,-r}$ since $\|L_{-r,-r}\|\le n$; with the current bound $\omega<2.371339$ (Alman-Duan-Vassilevska Williams-Xu-Xu-Zhou 2024) this is $O(n^{2.3714})$ bit operations. Without fast matrix multiplication, the sparse black-box determinant algorithm of Eberly-Giesbrecht-Giorgi-Storjohann-Villard (ISSAC 2007) runs in $\tilde O((n^{2-1/\omega}\phi(n)+n^{3-1/\omega})\log\|A\|)$ bit operations for a matrix with matrix-vector cost $\phi(n)$, i.e. $\tilde O(n^{2.66})$ bit operations here with $\omega=3$ and $\phi(n)=\tilde O(n)$. The problem is solved by either (i) an algorithm that outputs a 2-approximation of $\tau_r$ in $O(n^{\omega-c})$ bit operations for a constant $c>0$ on this class, the natural target being $\tilde O(n)$ word or bit operations matching the $O(m\log^{O(1)}n\log(1/\epsilon))$ Eulerian solvers of Cohen-Kelner-Kyng-Peebles-Peng-Rao-Sidford (2018) as the undirected determinant estimators of Durfee-Peebles-Peng-Rao (2017) and Liu-Peng-Yang (2025) do for SDDM matrices, or (ii) a fine-grained reduction showing that a 2-approximation of $\tau_r$ on polynomially mixing unit-weighted $O(n)$-arc digraphs is at least as hard as computing the determinant (or solving a linear system) of a general $n\times n$ integer matrix with polynomially bounded entries.

problems.sourceStatement: Determine the exact bit complexity of undirected integer-weighted Laplacian cofactor determinants and spanning-tree counts.
problems.wordDescription:
By Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem the cofactor $\det(L_{-r,-r})$ of a connected weighted graph Laplacian equals the weighted spanning-tree count, a positive integer with up to $\Theta(n\log n)$ bits (already $n^{n-2}$ for the unweighted complete graph). Nothing Laplacian-specific is known for computing it exactly: the best general bound is Storjohann's Las Vegas reduction of the integer determinant to integer matrix multiplication, about $\tilde O(n^{\omega}\log\|A\|)$ bit operations, which is $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ here since $\log\|L\| = O(\log n)$, and with $\omega < 2.371339$ this is below $n^{2.372}$. The sparse black-box determinant algorithm of Eberly, Giesbrecht, Giorgi, Storjohann and Villard costs $\tilde O((n^{2-1/\omega}m + n^{3-1/\omega})\log\|A\|)$ bit operations, i.e. about $\tilde O(n^{2.58})$ for $m = O(n)$, so sparsity alone does not currently beat the dense bound; only planar, bounded-genus and minor-free supports do better, via nested dissection in $O(n^{\omega/2})$ field operations.

This is exact symbolic computation rather than numerical linear algebra, so the approximate spanning-tree counters of problem 10 (Durfee, Peebles, Peng and Rao and their successors, which run in time polynomial in $1/\epsilon$) do not apply: pinning down an integer of $\Theta(n\log n)$ bits would need $\epsilon = 2^{-\Theta(n\log n)}$. Any exact speedup must control coefficient growth and modular reconstruction of an output as long as $n\log n$ bits, and must cope with the fact that the reduced Laplacian's Smith normal form (the critical group) can have many nontrivial invariant factors, e.g. $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{n-2}$ for $K_n$. The trivial lower bound is only the input-plus-output size $\Omega((m+n)\log n)$; no conditional hardness linking this problem to general integer determinants is known, and the question is whether Laplacian structure lets one get below $n^{\omega}$ on general graphs or whether the generic bound is the truth.

Input: a connected undirected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $m$ edges and integer edge weights $w_e \in [1, n^{10}]$, given as an edge list; its Laplacian $L$ has entries of magnitude at most $n^{11}$, so $\log\|L\| = O(\log n)$. For a specified root $r$, compute exactly the integer $\det(L_{-r,-r})$, which by the matrix-tree theorem equals $\sum_{T} \prod_{e \in T} w_e$ over spanning trees $T$. The output has $\Theta(n \log n)$ bits in the worst case: Hadamard's inequality gives $\det(L_{-r,-r}) \le \prod_{v \ne r} L_{vv} \le n^{11(n-1)}$, and the unweighted complete graph already has $n^{n-2}$ spanning trees, so no algorithm can run in $o(n \log n)$ bit operations and the trivial lower bound is $\Omega((m+n)\log n)$. Cost is measured in bit operations (not word operations, since intermediate integers have $\Theta(n \log n)$ bits), and one distinguishes deterministic algorithms, Las Vegas algorithms (always correct, expected running time) and Monte Carlo algorithms with success probability $1 - 1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. The error model is exact: an approximation is only acceptable if it determines the integer, i.e. a multiplicative $(1 \pm \epsilon)$ estimate is useless unless $\epsilon < 1/(2\det(L_{-r,-r}))$, which is $2^{-\Theta(n \log n)}$ in the worst case.

Baseline. No algorithm exploiting Laplacian structure is known on general graphs, so the baseline is the generic integer determinant. Dense: Storjohann (J. Complexity 2005, Theorem 59) computes $\det A$ for $A \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times n}$ in $(n^{\omega} \log\|A\|) \cdot \tilde O((\log n)^3 + (\log\log\|A\|)^2)$ bit operations Las Vegas, i.e. $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ here, which is $O(n^{2.372})$ with the current $\omega < 2.371339$ (Alman, Duan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou); the earlier bound of Kaltofen and Villard is $(n^{2.697263} \log\|A\|)^{1+o(1)}$ bit operations without relying on fast rectangular multiplication beyond $\omega$, and the deterministic textbook baseline (Chinese remaindering over $O(n)$ word-size primes) is $\tilde O(n^{\omega+1})$ bit operations. Sparse: Eberly, Giesbrecht, Giorgi, Storjohann and Villard compute the determinant of a black-box matrix with matrix-vector cost $\phi(n)$ in $\tilde O((n^{2-1/\omega} \phi(n) + n^{3-1/\omega}) \log\|A\|)$ bit operations; with $\phi(n) = \tilde O(m)$ this is $\tilde O(n^{2-1/\omega} m + n^{3-1/\omega})$, which for $m = O(n)$ is $\tilde O(n^{3-1/\omega}) \approx \tilde O(n^{2.58})$ and so does not beat $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ at the current $\omega$ (it does beat cubic algorithms when $\omega = 3$, giving $\tilde O(n^{2.66})$). Structured special cases: for planar or bounded-genus supports, nested dissection (Lipton, Rose and Tarjan over the reals for positive definite matrices; Alon and Yuster over any field, Las Vegas over finite fields) performs the elimination behind solving $Ax=b$ in $O(n^{\omega/2})$ field operations ($O(n^{3\omega/(\omega+3)})$ for fixed-minor-free supports), and Alon and Yuster state that for bounded integer entries the bit complexity is a further $\tilde O(n)$ factor larger; running this elimination modulo $O(n)$ word-size primes yields the exact determinant in $\tilde O(n^{1+\omega/2})$ bit operations on these graph classes, well below $n^{\omega}$, but nothing comparable is known for general sparse graphs. Target: either (a) an exact algorithm for every input in the class running in $\tilde O(n^{\omega - c})$ bit operations for a constant $c > 0$ (for instance $\tilde O(mn)$ for sparse graphs, the aspirational goal being near input-plus-output size $\tilde O(m + n)$), stating whether it is deterministic, Las Vegas or Monte Carlo; or (b) a fine-grained reduction showing that computing $\det A$ exactly for a general $A \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times n}$ with $\log\|A\| = O(\log n)$ (or another problem believed to need $n^{\omega - o(1)}$ time) reduces to exact reduced-Laplacian determinants of connected weighted graphs on $\tilde O(n)$ vertices, so that the generic $\tilde O(n^{\omega})$ bound is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors under standard assumptions.

problems.sourceStatement: Solve undirected Laplacian linear systems to 1/poly(n) accuracy in parallel in O(log^3 n) depth and m polylog(n) bit complexity.
problems.wordDescription:
Every nearly-linear-work parallel Laplacian solver with polylogarithmic depth descends from Peng and Spielman's sparse approximate inverse chains (2013), whose work and depth exponents were left unspecified, and from the sparsified block-Cholesky line of Lee, Peng and Spielman (2015) and Kyng, Lee, Peng, Sachdeva and Spielman (2016), which also handles connection Laplacians. The current frontier is the random-walk block-Cholesky solver of Sachdeva and Zhao (SPAA 2023): $O(m\log^3 n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ or $O((m+n\log^5 n)\log n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ work and $O(\log^2 n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ depth end to end, so at $\epsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ the depth is $O(\log^3 n\log\log n)$. The 2016 solver applies in $O((m+n\log^{1+o(1)}n)\log(1/\epsilon))$ work and the same depth, but its factorization takes $n^{o(1)}$ depth to build; the fully polylogarithmic 2015 construction needs $O(\log^6 n\log^4\log n)$ preprocessing depth. All of these bounds are stated for exact arithmetic on a PRAM; the only finite-precision analysis in this line is Spielman and Teng's for their sequential recursive solver, which needs $O(\log(\kappa/\epsilon)\log^{d}n)$ bits.

The question is therefore twofold: shave the remaining $\log\log n$ so that $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ accuracy is reached in $O(\log^3 n)$ depth with $O(m\log^3 n)$ word operations on $O(\log n)$-bit words, and prove that this holds under finite precision so that the bit complexity is genuinely $m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. The existence results of 2015 and 2016 show what is ultimately possible: every Laplacian has an $O(n)$-nonzero approximate Cholesky factorization that can be applied in $O(n)$ work and $O(\log n\log^2\log n)$ depth, but it is only known to be computable in polynomial time. Baumann and Kyng (SPAA 2024) and Baumann and Zoecklein (2026) give simpler parallel elimination and solver-free parallel sparsification frameworks aimed at practical solvers, but neither states explicit bounds that beat Sachdeva and Zhao.
problems.mathematicalConditions:
Let $G$ be a connected undirected graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges and integer edge weights in $[1,n^{10}]$, let $L$ be its Laplacian (so $\log\kappa(L)=O(\log n)$), and let $b\perp\mathbf{1}$. The task is to output, with probability at least $1-1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$, a vector $\tilde x$ with $\|\tilde x-L^\dagger b\|_L\le\epsilon\|L^\dagger b\|_L$ for $\epsilon=n^{-c}$, any fixed $c>0$. Cost is measured end to end (constructing any preconditioner or factorization plus applying it) as work and depth on a CREW PRAM whose primitive operations act on $O(\log n)$-bit words; a complete solution must include a finite-precision analysis showing that $O(\log n)$-bit words (or polylogarithmically many bits) suffice, so that the bit complexity is the word-operation count times a polylogarithmic factor. Current best, in exact arithmetic: Sachdeva and Zhao (arXiv:2304.14345, SPAA 2023) give $O(m\log^3 n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ or $O((m+n\log^5 n)\log n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ work and $O(\log^2 n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ depth, i.e. $O(\log^3 n\log\log n)$ depth at $\epsilon=n^{-c}$. Kyng, Lee, Peng, Sachdeva and Spielman (arXiv:1512.01892, STOC 2016) apply their sparsified-multigrid solver in $O((m+n\log^{1+o(1)}n)\log(1/\epsilon))$ work and $O(\log^2 n\log\log n\log(1/\epsilon))$ depth after $O(m\log n+n\log^{2+o(1)}n)$ work but $O(n^{o(1)})$ depth of preprocessing; Lee, Peng and Spielman (arXiv:1506.08204, Theorem 9.2) build a fully polylogarithmic solver in $O(\log^6 n\log^4\log n)$ depth; Peng and Spielman (arXiv:1311.3286, STOC 2014) gave the first nearly-linear-work polylogarithmic-depth solver with unspecified exponents. None of these four papers analyzes finite precision; the only such analysis is Spielman and Teng's for their sequential recursive solver, needing $O(\log(\kappa(L)/\epsilon)\log^{d}n)$ bits.

Target (solves the problem): an algorithm meeting the above specification with end-to-end depth $O(\log^2 n\log(1/\epsilon))$, which is $O(\log^3 n)$ at $\epsilon=n^{-c}$, and total work $O(m\log^3 n\log(1/\epsilon))$ word operations, together with a finite-precision analysis with $O(\log n)$-bit words, giving $m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ bit complexity; this removes the $\log\log n$ factor from both the depth and the sparse-graph work of Sachdeva and Zhao while adding the missing bit accounting. Partial credit: either the depth improvement or the finite-precision analysis for an existing polylogarithmic-depth solver at the Sachdeva-Zhao bounds. Ultimate target: after $m\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$-work, $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$-depth preprocessing, solve in $O(m\log(1/\epsilon))$ work and $O(\log n\cdot\mathrm{polyloglog}(n)\cdot\log(1/\epsilon))$ depth, matching the existence bound of Lee, Peng and Spielman for $O(n)$-nonzero approximate Cholesky factorizations, which are currently only known to be computable in polynomial time.
